title: Value Types
description: Explore C# value types in depth — integers, floating-point numbers, char, bool, structs, and how they differ from reference types in memory and behavior.

data.text: C# types fall into two broad categories: **value types** and **reference types**. Value types store their data directly in memory, usually on the **stack**. When you assign a value type to another variable, C# makes a complete copy — the two variables are entirely independent after the assignment.

Understanding value types is critical because they behave differently from reference types when you pass them to methods, assign them to other variables, or compare them. Getting this wrong is one of the most common sources of bugs for beginners.

data.text: C# provides several built-in (primitive) value types. Each has a specific size in memory and a defined range of valid values. Choosing the right type helps your program use memory efficiently and avoids unexpected overflow errors.

rows: Default integer type; most common choice

data.text: `int` is the most commonly used integer type in C#. It offers a good balance of range and performance. The compiler treats bare integer literals (like `42`) as `int` by default. Use `long` when you need to store numbers larger than 2 billion, and use `byte` when memory efficiency matters (such as in large arrays).

rows: Financial calculations where precision is critical

data.text: `float` and `double` use the IEEE 754 standard and are extremely fast but can have tiny rounding errors. For example, `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3` in floating-point. `decimal` avoids this by using a base-10 representation, making it ideal for money calculations.

data.text: The `char` type holds a single Unicode character (16 bits in C#). It uses single quotes: `'A'`. The `bool` type holds either `true` or `false` and is essential for conditions, loops, and logical operations.

data.title: char and bool in Practice

data.text: You can define your own value types using the `struct` keyword. Structs are useful for small, immutable data structures that represent a single value — like a 2D point, a complex number, or a coordinate. Unlike classes, structs cannot inherit from other structs or classes (except `System.ValueType`), and they always have a default parameterless constructor.

data.title: Value Semantics
data.text: When you assign a value type (including structs) to another variable, C# copies every bit of data. Modifying the copy does NOT affect the original. This is called value semantics and is the core difference from reference types.

data.title: Good candidates for structs:
items: Immutable data that represents a single value
Types that would otherwise be passed by value frequently (e.g., `Point`, `Complex`, `Rectangle`)
Performance-critical code where heap allocation overhead matters

data.title: Avoid structs when:
items: The struct is large (more than 16 bytes)
You need a parameterless constructor that does real work
The type will be boxed frequently (cast to object or interface)

items.hint: Anything that stores its data directly is a value type.

items.text: I understand that value types are copied on assignment
items.hint: Assigning one to another creates a separate copy.

items.text: I know when to use struct vs class
items.hint: Small, immutable, single-value types are good struct candidates.

items.text: I can explain the difference between float, double, and decimal
items.hint: Use decimal for money; double for most other math.

data.title: Exercise: Create a Temperature Struct
data.description: Build a struct that represents a temperature in Celsius, with methods to convert to Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
steps: Create a struct called `Temperature` with a `Celsius` property (double)
Add a constructor that accepts a Celsius value
Add a read-only property `Fahrenheit` that returns Celsius * 9/5 + 32
Add a read-only property `Kelvin` that returns Celsius + 273.15
Override `ToString()` to return a formatted string like "25°C / 77°F / 298.15K"
In `Main`, create two `Temperature` values, copy one to another, modify the copy, and show the original is unchanged
data.expectedOutcome: A working `Temperature` struct with conversion properties and demonstrated value semantics when copied.

items.question: Are all primitive types value types?
items.answer: Almost all. `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `char`, and `bool` are value types. `string` and `object` are reference types, which is a common exception that surprises beginners.

items.question: What is boxing and unboxing?
items.answer: Boxing is when a value type is wrapped inside an `object` reference, copying it to the heap. Unboxing extracts it back. Both have a performance cost and should be avoided in performance-sensitive code.

items.question: Should I make everything a struct for speed?
items.answer: No. Structs only provide a benefit for small, frequently-copied types. Large structs are slower because copying them is expensive. Microsoft recommends structs be under 16 bytes.

items.question: Can structs be null?
items.answer: No — unless you use `Nullable<T>` syntax: `Point? p = null;`. The `?` suffix wraps the value type in a nullable wrapper that can represent null.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Value types store data directly on the stack
Assignment creates a full copy (value semantics)
Built-in value types: int, long, float, double, decimal, char, bool
Use decimal for financial calculations to avoid rounding errors
Structs let you define custom value types
Good structs are small (under 16 bytes) and immutable
data.takeaway: Value types are fast, efficient, and copied by value. Use them for small, self-contained pieces of data.
